items.title: Selections over collections
items.bodyMarkdown: A single-chapter fixture used to exercise the content pipeline end to end.

items.title: Selecting records without changing them
items.bodyMarkdown:
A support desk constantly asks narrow questions of a wide list: how many tickets are open, which ones belong to this customer, which breached their response time. Each of those is a selection over the same array, and none of them should change the array itself.

JavaScript gives you `filter` for exactly this. It walks the array, keeps the records your predicate accepts, and hands back a **new** array. The original is untouched, which means the caller can ask a second question of the same data and get an answer that still makes sense.
objectives: Select matching records from an array with filter.
Explain why a selection must not modify its input.
commonMistakes: Using `forEach` with a counter and accidentally editing the records while counting them.
Comparing with `==` so that a status of `null` or `0` matches unexpectedly.
Assuming `filter` edits the array in place and then wondering why the original still has every record.
items.summaryMarkdown: `filter` selects; it never edits. Keep selections pure so the same data can answer several questions in a row.

items.title: Count open support tickets
items.bodyMarkdown: Practice selecting records without changing the input.
items.promptMarkdown: Return the number of tickets whose status is exactly `open`. Do not mutate the input. Status comparisons are case-sensitive.
hints: Separate selecting the matching tickets from counting them.
Array.filter returns a new array containing only the records that match.
Filter by ticket.status === 'open', then read the resulting array's length.

solution.explanationMarkdown: Filtering selects matching records without changing the original array, and the resulting length is the count. An empty input produces zero. A loop with a counter is equally valid.

items.title: Diagnose a shared nested record
items.bodyMarkdown: Read the code and decide what the spread actually copied.
items.promptMarkdown: A dispatcher copies a ticket with `const copy = { ...ticket }` and then edits `copy.customer.name`. The original ticket changes too. Why?
hints: Ask how many levels deep the copy went.
A spread copies the top-level properties only; nested objects are shared by reference.
`copy.customer` and `ticket.customer` point at the same object, so editing one is editing both.

solution.modelAnswer: The spread is a shallow copy, so the nested customer object is shared.
solution.explanationMarkdown: A spread copies each top-level property value. For a nested object that value is a reference, so the copy and the original point at the same customer record. Copying the nested object as well fixes it.

options.textMarkdown: The spread copied only the top level, so `customer` is shared.
options.explanationMarkdown: Correct. A spread copies one level; nested values stay shared references.

options.textMarkdown: Object spread does not copy anything.
options.explanationMarkdown: It does copy: `copy` is a new object. The issue is only that the copy is one level deep.

options.textMarkdown: `const` prevents the copy from being modified.
options.explanationMarkdown: `const` stops the binding being reassigned. It does not freeze the object it refers to.

options.textMarkdown: Only `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` can copy an object at all.
options.explanationMarkdown: That produces a deep copy, but it is not the only way, and it silently drops dates and functions.

items.title: Explain why the filter helper stays pure
items.bodyMarkdown: Put the reasoning into your own words; the criteria are shown after you answer.
items.promptMarkdown: A colleague proposes changing `countOpen` to also mark each open ticket as seen. Explain what that would cost the caller and what you would suggest instead.
hints: Think about what the caller assumes when it passes its own array in.
A function that both answers a question and changes data is hard to reuse and hard to test.
Separate the query from the command: return the count, and let a separate function record that tickets were seen.

solution.modelAnswer: Marking tickets inside countOpen makes the function impure: calling it twice would change the data, callers could no longer use it for a simple count, and tests would need to rebuild fixtures between assertions. Keep the count as a pure query and move the marking into an explicit separate operation.
solution.explanationMarkdown: The point is separating a query from a command. A pure count can be called anywhere, cached and tested trivially. Once it also mutates, every caller inherits that side effect whether it wanted it or not.

criteria: Identifies that the function would no longer be pure, because it changes data the caller owns.
Names a concrete consequence, such as repeat calls differing, or tests needing fresh fixtures each time.
Proposes separating the count from the marking rather than adding a flag argument.
grading.modelAnswerMarkdown: Marking tickets inside `countOpen` makes it impure. Calling it twice would produce different data, so callers can no longer treat it as a simple question, and every test needs a fresh fixture. I would keep `countOpen` as a pure query and add a separate `markTicketsSeen` operation the caller invokes deliberately.

items.title: What does filter return?
items.bodyMarkdown: Recall the return value and its effect on the original array.
items.promptMarkdown: What does `Array.prototype.filter` return, and what happens to the array you called it on?
items.answerMarkdown: It returns a **new** array containing the elements the predicate accepted. The original array is not modified.
items.explanationMarkdown: This is the property that makes selections composable: the source data survives, so you can ask another question of it.

items.title: Spot the impure selection
items.bodyMarkdown: Apply the idea to unfamiliar code.
items.promptMarkdown: A helper is written as `function urgent(t) { t.forEach(x => x.seen = true); return t.filter(x => x.priority === 1); }`. Name the defect and the symptom a caller would report.
items.answerMarkdown: It mutates every ticket by setting `seen` before selecting. A caller would report that simply asking for urgent tickets marked the whole queue as seen.
items.explanationMarkdown: The `filter` half is fine. The `forEach` above it is a hidden side effect, so the function is a command pretending to be a query.

items.title: Selections and immutability placement check
items.bodyMarkdown: Five separately authored items covering this chapter. No hints are shown until you submit.

items.promptMarkdown: Given `[3, 8, 2, 9]`, what does `nums.filter(n => n > 4)` evaluate to, and what is `nums` afterwards?

options.textMarkdown: `[8, 9]`, and `nums` still has four elements.
options.explanationMarkdown: Correct: a new array of the accepted values, source unchanged.

options.textMarkdown: `[8, 9]`, and `nums` now has two elements.
options.explanationMarkdown: filter does not remove elements from the source array.

options.textMarkdown: `[3, 2]`, and `nums` is unchanged.
options.explanationMarkdown: The predicate keeps values greater than 4, not the others.

options.textMarkdown: `true`, because the predicate returns a boolean.
options.explanationMarkdown: The predicate returns booleans; filter itself returns an array.

items.explanationMarkdown: filter builds a new array from the values the predicate accepted and leaves the source alone.

items.promptMarkdown: Which of these makes a function impure?

options.textMarkdown: It writes a property on an object it received as an argument.
options.explanationMarkdown: Yes: it changes state the caller owns.

options.textMarkdown: It reads a property of its argument.
options.explanationMarkdown: Reading is fine; purity restricts changes, not access.

options.textMarkdown: It appends to an array declared outside the function.
options.explanationMarkdown: Yes: that is an observable side effect outside its own scope.

options.textMarkdown: It declares a local variable.
options.explanationMarkdown: Local state is invisible to callers and keeps the function pure.

items.explanationMarkdown: Impurity is about observable change outside the function, not about how much work happens inside it.

items.promptMarkdown: After `const b = { ...a }`, which statement changes `a` as well as `b`?

options.textMarkdown: `b.meta.tag = "x"` where `a.meta` is an object.
options.explanationMarkdown: Correct: the nested object is shared between the two copies.

options.textMarkdown: `b.title = "x"` where `a.title` is a string.
options.explanationMarkdown: Top-level properties were copied, so this only affects `b`.
That reassigns the binding `b`; `a` is untouched.

options.textMarkdown: None of them, because the spread is a deep copy.
options.explanationMarkdown: The spread copies one level only.

items.explanationMarkdown: A spread copies top-level values. Nested objects are copied by reference, so both records share them.

items.promptMarkdown: A colleague replaces `list.filter(fn)` with a `for` loop that calls `list.splice()` when a record does not match. What breaks?

options.textMarkdown: The caller’s array is emptied of non-matching records, and the loop skips elements as indices shift.
options.explanationMarkdown: Both problems are real: splice mutates in place and shifts every later index.

options.textMarkdown: Nothing; splice and filter are equivalent.
options.explanationMarkdown: splice edits in place, filter returns a new array.

options.textMarkdown: Only performance changes.
options.explanationMarkdown: Correctness changes first: the source array is modified.

options.textMarkdown: The loop throws because splice cannot be used on arrays.
options.explanationMarkdown: splice is a standard array method; it works, which is exactly why the defect is quiet.

items.explanationMarkdown: Mutating a collection while iterating over it shifts the indices under the loop, and it destroys data the caller still needed.

items.promptMarkdown: Which predicate counts only tickets whose status is exactly the lowercase word `open`?

options.textMarkdown: `t => t.status === "open"`
options.explanationMarkdown: Strict equality against the exact string is what the requirement asks for.

options.textMarkdown: `t => t.status == "open"`
options.explanationMarkdown: Loose equality is unnecessary here and invites coercion surprises elsewhere.

options.textMarkdown: `t => t.status.toLowerCase() === "open"`
options.explanationMarkdown: That also accepts `Open` and `OPEN`, which the requirement excludes.

options.textMarkdown: `t => t.status`
options.explanationMarkdown: That accepts every non-empty status, not just `open`.

items.explanationMarkdown: The requirement is case-sensitive, so normalising the case would accept records it should reject.
